new_statements.quote: Every word of two or more syllables (after you remove certain never-stressed word endings) is stressed on one of its last three syllables. Given the written word, you can tell which of the last three syllables is stressed by applying this Rule of Stress: If any syllable has a stressmark, that syllable is the one that is stressed. Otherwise, the word is stressed on the vocalic before the last consonant in the word (ignoring consonants in the word endings -as, -en, -ent, -er(s), -eux, -ic, -ica(s), -ici, -ilor, -laiset, -mint, -p(h)äts, and -sqab, if the word ends with one of those); If there is no such vocalic, the word is stressed on its first vocalic.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically marked by a diacritic when irregular; otherwise it falls on the last closed syllable of the word (the vowel before the last consonant), computed after stripping a closed list of never-stressed suffixes, and always within the last three syllables; a word with no closed syllable is stressed on its first vowel. Default stress can therefore be final (cunceßetz), penultimate (cunceßent) or antepenultimate (cunceßadamint), as the ATLO page spells out.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; in hyphenated words each element carries its own stress (parta-t-o stressed on par and o).
new_statements.exceptions: Any stressmarked vowel overrides the rule; the never-stressed endings -as, -en, -ent, -er(s), -eux, -ic, -ica(s), -ici, -ilor, -laiset, -mint, -p(h)äts, -sqab are ignored (only the one the word actually ends with); words with no vocalic before a consonant (mici, ricas) take initial stress; optional unmarked final stress on 3sg future verbs (lirarha; serà obligatorily final); acest and vidarh optionally initial-stressed. The ATLO talossan.com page adds a slightly different ending list (-esch(en), -eu(x), -lor, -ttä) and umlaut vowels ä ö ü counting as stress-attracting, and cites embù and azul as optionally initial.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for reading the standard orthography (Modern Orthography, post-2007) of a constructed language; the rule is stated over written words, and 'consonant' includes unstressmarked i/u before a vowel. Hyphenated compounds are stressed on each part separately (6.2). No phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Talossan is an artificial language (Glottolog family 'Artificial Language', glottocode talo1253, ISO tzl). The quoted rule is the Kingdom of Talossa's standard 'Modern Orthography' adopted by the CÚG decree of 12 December 2007; pre-2007 'Classic' Talossan (Madison 1996 grammar) had no general stress rule and marked stress with assorted diacritics, and some writers (notably in the Republic of Talossa) retain that convention. Same glottocode; no separate code for the orthographic varieties. The catalog owner may want to exclude conlangs regardless.

new_statements.quote: 2014, A2014.1: "If any syllable of a word contains a stress-marked vowel, then that is the syllable that is stressed. Otherwise, the syllable to be stressed is determined by applying this Rule of Stress: Stress falls on the syllable containing the final vowel that is either marked with an umlaut (ä, ö, or ü) or followed by a consonant, after ignoring word-terminal -s and the word endings -en(s), -ent(s), -er(s), -esch(en), -eu(x), -ica(s), -ic(i), -(esch)laiset(s), -lor, -mint(s), -p(h)äts, and -sqab(s) (if the word ends with one of these). For the purposes of this rule, an i or u that immediately follows any vowel, and an e that immediately follows an a, are treated as consonants." NOTE 1: "In words like mici (= 'crumbs'), troica (= 'trio'), and ricas (= 'windrows'), in which the stress rule fails to identify a stressed syllable, stress falls on the first syllable." 2011, 1.1 (Talossan): "L'emfasiçù tomba sür el sülaval qi cuntent la letra vocal avant qe la “braça” final del moct: Ingen consonant eda grupa dels consonants c'e'n braça, salva qe s c'e'n braça solamint osprei qe n eda ö eda ü. Ingen glideu (salva qe el u in eu) c'e'n braça." 2010, 1.1 (Talossan): "3. L'emfasiçù tomba sür el final vocal läxhir in el moct (eda schi acest vocal isch pärts d'iens polüftunc, sür el compläts ftunc qi cuntent acest final vocal läxhir)."
new_statements.translation: 2011, 1.1: "Stress falls on the syllable containing the vowel letter before the final 'brace' of the word: any consonant or consonant group is a brace, except that s is a brace only after n or ö or ü. Any glide (except the u in eu) is a brace." 2010, 1.1: "3. Stress falls on the final strong vowel in the word (or, if that vowel is part of a polyphthong, on the whole phthong containing that final strong vowel)." (2010 adds: the weak, i.e. non-strong, vowels are those in the endings -V, -iV, -Va, -eu, -Veu, -ic, -icV, -er, -(i/u)ent; the suffixes -mint, -laiset(s), -p(h)äts, -sqab(s) are always unstressed and are ignored; Note 2: in words like frulor, mici, diceux, vea, ricas, where all vowels are weak by the rule, stress falls on the first vowel.)

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing 2007 statement (weight-sensitive: rightmost closed/heavy syllable after stripping never-stressed endings, orthographic marks override) but these are the amended rules that superseded the 2007 Rule of Stress. The 2010 Stätsmint (printed p. 1, p. 4) says the 2007 rule had deficiencies (it required marking naturally final-stressed words like ospréi, spicarái and irregular pártis, Llimbaziúa) and adopts a new rule under which those words are regular and unmarked. The 2010-2014 rule no longer states a three-syllable window (the 2007 statement's 'one of its last three syllables'); it names the final strong/closed or umlauted vowel directly and adds the first-syllable fal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (unmarked) stress is computed from the spelling: strip a closed list of inherently unstressed endings (-mint, -laiset, -p(h)äts, -sqab, and in 2014 also -en, -ent, -er, -esch, -eu(x), -ica, -ic(i), -lor, final -s), then stress the rightmost syllable whose vowel is 'strong' — followed by a consonant (closed syllable; post-vocalic i/u and a+e count as consonants) or an umlauted vowel ä/ö/ü. A final open vowel is never stressed by default. If no syllable qualifies (all vowels weak), stress falls on the first syllable. Any written stress mark (acute/grave/circumflex) overrides the rule and marks lexically irregular stress. Between 2010 and 2014 the formulation was reworded three times ('final strong vowel' 2010; 'vowel before the final brace' 2011; 'final vowel followed by a consonant or umlauted' 2014) with slightly different ending lists, but the placement principle is the same.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any of the three Arestadas.
new_statements.exceptions: Written stress marks mark irregular (lexical) stress and override the rule. 2014 Notes: optional final-syllable stress on 3sg future verbs (lirarha) is unmarked, but ischà, säperà, serà have obligatory marked final stress; azul, acest, vidarh, embù may optionally take first-syllable stress; in apostrophe abbreviations stress follows the full spelling (éu lament', treslais't). A2014.4: number words qátor, séifet, bísquinc, úndaveint, þúsund have irregular stress usually written unmarked. A2014.5 lists 34 words with irregular stress on an umlauted vowel. 2011 1.2-1.4: stress shifts under pluralisation (regipäts -> regipätsilor stressed on ä; solas -> solasen stressed on a; aspáragosch -> asparagoschen regular on o) while foren -> fórens, pengö -> péngös retain stem stress and take a mark; verbs stressed irregularly on the stem keep that stress only in the infinitive (sâparh -> säpeveu); monosyllables keep stem stress under prefixation. 2010 1.3: 11-18 (ûndesch.. vuídesch) and úndaveint marked irregular; suffixes -osis, -eria/-erie, -ia no longer stress-marked.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe the same constructed language (Talossan, tzl). Work 1 explicitly covers the pre-Arestada-2007 'Old Spelling' standard; work 0 covers the post-2007 CÚG standard as amended in 2010, 2011 and 2014 (the 2010 and 2011 Arestadas are written in Talossan, the 2014 one in English). Talossan is a constructed language of the Kingdom of Talossa micronation (Milwaukee), not a natural language.

new_statements.quote: NOTE: This page is specific to "Old Spelling" -- that is, the orthography of the Talossan language before the Arestada of 12 December 2007. [...] (The following is taken, with kind permission, from materials provided by Sir Tomás Garecéir, UrGP.) Stress is a tricky matter in Talossan, like English, as which syllable takes the stress can vary widely from word to word and there are no definite rules. Some general guidelines, however, can be offered. The stressed syllable is most often the last or the next-to-last (penultimate), less often the third from the end (antepenultimate), and only rarely further back than that. The stressed syllable is often indicated with a written accent. [...] If there is no accented vowel in the word and it does not end in -iun, then the word is probably accented on the penultimate syllable. [...] If none of the preceding rules apply, then the word is most likely accented on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Differs in type from the existing 2007 statement (and from work 0): it says there are 'no definite rules' and stress 'can vary widely from word to word', giving only tendencies with a penultimate default, whereas the 2007-2014 Arestadas state a deterministic weight-like rule with marked lexical exceptions. The page itself says it describes the pre-Arestada-2007 orthography and was to be updated, so the disagreement is diachronic (superseded standard), not a competing description of the same standard; it agrees with the catalog that stress lies within the last three syllables and that written accents mark it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pre-2007 ('Old Spelling') description: stress is lexically variable with no definite rules; it falls mostly on the final or penultimate syllable, less often the antepenult, rarely earlier, and is usually shown by a written accent (the last accented vowel is stressed, with listed ending exceptions). Certain endings always take stress (-at, -ats, -esc, -eschti, -etz, -iun, infinitive -ar/-arë), some are stressed on the antepenult (-amînt, -âmînt, -ici, -ìci, -ilor, -ipäts), negative prefixes în-/ûn- are never stressed, and the residual default is the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Endings -â, -âs, -escù, -ìci, -mînt, -päts, -phäts, -üm, -üs and prefixes în-/ûn- do not carry the written-accent stress; -escù is stressed on the e despite the mark on ù; double ii is usually stressed; written accents on a root do not move when a suffix is added even though stress shifts (escláv -> esclávátx stressed on -átx).
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe the same constructed language (Talossan, tzl). Work 1 explicitly covers the pre-Arestada-2007 'Old Spelling' standard; work 0 covers the post-2007 CÚG standard as amended in 2010, 2011 and 2014 (the 2010 and 2011 Arestadas are written in Talossan, the 2014 one in English). Talossan is a constructed language of the Kingdom of Talossa micronation (Milwaukee), not a natural language.

readall_conflicts: The pre-2007 'Old Spelling' page (work 1, text by Tomás Gariçéir, last modified Jan 2008) says Talossan stress has 'no definite rules' and varies lexically, defaulting to the penult and marked with written accents; the CÚG Arestadas of 2007 (existing statement), 2010, 2011 and 2014 (work 0) instead state a deterministic default rule (rightmost closed-syllable or umlauted vowel after stripping never-stressed endings, first syllable if none qualifies) with orthographic stress marks reserved for lexical irregulars. The 2010 Arestada's Stätsmint explicitly amends the 2007 rule because it forced marks on naturally final-stressed words (ospréi, spicarái) and on pártis, Llimbaziúa; so the 2007 and 2010-2014 formulations differ in detail (ending lists, no three-syllable window after 2010) though not in type. Both conflicts are diachronic revisions of a regulated conlang standard rather than descriptive disagreements.

sources.note: Section 6 'Stress', 6.3 'The Stress Rule' (p. 10): a stressmarked syllable is stressed; otherwise stress falls on the vocalic before the last consonant of the word, ignoring a closed list of never-stressed endings; if no such vocalic, the first vocalic; always within the last three syllables. Notes: i/u before a vowel count as consonants; optional unmarked final stress on 3sg future verbs; acest, vidarh optionally initial-stressed.

States that the Arestada sür Speliçaziun of 12 December 2007 'instituted a rule for stress that allowed many extraneous stressmarks to be omitted' and standardized stressmarks (acute/grave on a e i o u); lists later Arestadas 2010/XXXI, 2011/XXXII, 2014/XXXV (Arest10/11/) not downloaded.
